title: Baby Back Ribs
subtitle: Glazed pork back ribs with a sweet-spiced crust
excerpt: Baby back ribs are the smaller, leaner rack cut from the top of the ribcage near the spine. They cook faster than spare ribs and take a glaze beautifully in the final stage. These are rubbed, braised until tender, then finished with a sweet and sticky coating.
sourceNotes: Baby back rib technique based on standard American barbecue oven-braise method. The three-stage cook (rub, covered braise, glazed finish) is the widely used home approach.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze cooked and glazed rack wrapped tightly in foil. Reheat at 180°C covered for 20 minutes, then uncover to re-glaze.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cook the low phase a day ahead and refrigerate. Finish with the glaze for 20 minutes at 200°C when ready to serve.

content.text: Baby back ribs are the shorter, more curved rack from the upper ribcage, with less fat than spare ribs and more meat between the bones. They cook in about two and a half hours in the oven and take a sticky glaze better than any other rib cut. The method is three stages: rub and seal with foil, braise at low heat until the meat gives, then finish uncovered with a sweet coating painted on in layers.
Heat the oven to 150°C (fan 130°C / gas mark 2). Remove the membrane from the bone side of the {{pork-ribs}}: loosen a corner with a blunt knife, then grip and peel it off with kitchen paper.

Mix together all the rub ingredients: {{paprika-smoked}}, {{dark-brown-sugar}}, {{garlic-powder}}, {{onion-powder}}, {{sea-salt-flakes}}, and {{black-pepper}}. Pat the rack dry and coat thoroughly on both sides with the rub.
Place the rack meat side up on a foil-lined baking tray and cover tightly with foil. Cook at 150°C for two hours.

Combine {{ketchup}}, {{honey}}, {{dark-brown-sugar}}, {{cider-vinegar}}, {{worcestershire-sauce}}, and {{garlic-powder}} in a small saucepan. Stir over medium heat for three minutes until slightly thickened. Taste and adjust the balance of sweet and sour if needed.
Remove the foil. Increase the oven to 200°C (fan 180°C / gas mark 6). Brush a generous layer of glaze over the meat side of the rack. Return to the oven uncovered for 10 minutes.

Brush on a second layer of glaze and cook for another 10 to 15 minutes until the surface is sticky and caramelised with a few dark edges. Watch carefully at this stage: the sugar in the glaze burns fast.
Rest for ten minutes, then cut between the bones to separate. Serve any remaining glaze as a dipping sauce on the side.

items.symptom: The glaze burns before the ribs are caramelised
items.cause: Oven too hot, or glaze applied too early.
items.fix: Apply the glaze only after the full two-hour covered phase. Watch the ribs through the oven door: 20 to 25 minutes total uncovered is usually enough.

items.symptom: The meat is still tough after two hours
items.cause: Baby back ribs can vary in thickness. The foil seal wasn't tight enough.
items.fix: Crimp the foil tightly around all edges. Add another 20 minutes covered, then test by pressing the meat with a finger through a fold of foil.

items.symptom: The glaze is thin and doesn't stick
items.cause: Not reduced enough, or applied while the rack was still steaming.
items.fix: Simmer the glaze an extra two minutes to thicken before applying. Let the rack sit out of the oven for two minutes before brushing.

items.symptom: The rack curves and doesn't lie flat
items.cause: Baby back ribs naturally arch. Not a problem.
items.fix: Cut the rack in half before cooking to fit the tray, or prop up the ends with small rolls of foil to keep it level.

content.text: Baby back ribs are the most popular rib cut in American restaurants and home cooking because they're leaner and cook faster than spare ribs. The name comes from the fact that they're the shorter bones from the top of the rack, not that they come from a young pig. Serve with coleslaw, sweet potato fries, or corn on the cob. The glaze recipe here is a straightforward sweet-sour American style: add a teaspoon of chipotle paste to the glaze if you want heat.
